title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 19: A New Year's Wish
keywords: man is restless till he rests in God
primary_topics: Chapter 19 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's New Year message for 1991 in the Rotary Balita of January 3, 1991, which moves from the collapse of Soviet atheism to a single personal wish: 'that I become more open to Him and His word so that daily, I may do only what He wills for me'

The thaw in the once-atheist empire as his opening evidence: Gorbachev visiting the Pope and admitting that suppressing Czechoslovakia, invading Afghanistan and excluding religion from Russian life were mistakes; perestroika and glasnost as 'just the beginning'; even the first Rotary Club of Moscow

His anthropology: man is everywhere the same, his spirit 'created in the image of God, be he Russian, American or Filipino,' and that spirit 'hungers and thirsts for fulfillment' which drugs, wine, wealth, power and 'mob adulation' can never satisfy

His own conversion of outlook: from a 'restless past' in which God was 'someone apart and unreachable' and prayer unnecessary, to a 'personal God' -- Jesus as friend, guide and consoler -- addressed in thought every morning on waking
sub_topics: He begins with successive admissions of surprise -- that the Soviet Union would reconcile with Christianity, that Gorbachev would visit the Pope, and that he would call the exclusion of religion from Russian life a mistake
He reads perestroika and glasnost as only 'the beginning of the thaw,' now followed by free enterprise, individual initiative and economic liberalism sweeping 'that once-upon-a-time caged empire'
He notes that even Rotary 'made history' with the organization of the first Rotary Club of Moscow that year
He contrasts this with his earlier image of the Soviets as 'heartless men who were constantly chasing James Bond,' defeated by 'the superior and oftentimes romantic wiles of Agent 007'
With the Iron Curtain lifted, he generalizes: man's spirit is made in God's image whether Russian, American or Filipino, and hungers for fulfillment 'in this life as well as in the next'
He catalogues the false satisfactions -- 'drugs, women, wine and wealth,' 'a madding lust for power,' 'the sunshine of mob adulation' -- and judges them 'self-destructive and at best, temporary'
He distinguishes 'the human in man' from 'the more overwhelming spirit in man,' which such pleasures can never satisfy
He invokes St. Augustine -- 'man is restless till he rests in God' -- and concludes that he 'did not have to be a Russian' to learn he cannot separate religion from daily life

He states the integration in a chain of clauses: he cannot 'dichotomize my work from my faith,' must live each day 'with the same eternal faith and enduring values,' and holds 'my Christianity and my humanity are one inseparable whole'
He confesses his 'restless past,' when he thought God 'apart and unreachable,' prayer pointless because God already knew his needs, and his problems too insignificant to bother Him with

He describes his present practice: waking each morning and speaking with Jesus in his thoughts, to thank, praise and ask for open eyes and heart -- 'it is not what I ask of Him that really matters; it is what He tells me I should do'
He closes with the single wish for 1991 and applies the Lord's prayer's 'Thy will be done' to his life, family, career, the Rotary Club of Manila and his country

stances.claim: The Soviet turn -- Gorbachev conceding to the Pope that suppressing Czechoslovakia, invading Afghanistan and excluding religion from Russian life were mistakes -- shows that a state cannot permanently exclude God from human life.
stances.rhetorical_move: escalating-astonishment: three stacked admissions ('I never thought... More incredibly... And much more than that') that build the political fact into a spiritual lesson

stances.claim: Greed for money, power and glorification is 'self-destructive and at best, temporary'; it may please 'the human in man' but can never satisfy 'the more overwhelming spirit in man,' which rests only in God.
stances.rhetorical_move: catalogue-then-verdict: listing the worldly substitutes before ruling them all insufficient, sealed by St. Augustine's line on restlessness

stances.claim: Faith cannot be compartmentalized -- he 'cannot dichotomize my work from my faith,' and 'my Christianity and my humanity are one inseparable whole.'
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-testimony as proof: arguing the universal point from his own change of mind rather than from doctrine

stances.claim: Prayer is not a matter of asking but of listening -- 'it is not what I ask of Him that really matters; it is what He tells me I should do that truly matters' -- so his one wish for the year is openness to God's will.
stances.rhetorical_move: reversal of the conventional New Year's wish: a single request for openness rather than a list of things wanted

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reprints Artemio V. Panganiban's New Year message for 1991, published in the Rotary Balita of January 3, 1991. He opened with stacked admissions of surprise: that the Soviet Union, 'while embracing and professing communism,' would reconcile with Christianity; that Mikhail Gorbachev would visit the Pope and call the suppression of Czechoslovakia and the invasion of Afghanistan mistakes; and, most of all, that Gorbachev would tell the Pope 'it was a mistake to exclude religion from the life of the Russian people.' Perestroika and glasnost, he wrote, 'were just the beginning of the thaw,' with free enterprise and economic liberalism now sweeping 'that once-upon-a-time caged empire' -- and even Rotary making history with the first Rotary Club of Moscow. He contrasted this with his earlier picture of the Soviets as 'heartless men who were constantly chasing James Bond,' and, with the Iron Curtain lifted, generalized that man is everywhere the same, his spirit created in God's image 'be he Russian, American or Filipino,' hungering and thirsting for fulfillment. Some try to satisfy that hunger with 'drugs, women, wine and wealth,' some with 'a madding lust for power,' some by bathing in 'the sunshine of mob adulation'; but such greed is 'self-destructive and at best, temporary,' pleasing 'the human in man' while never satisfying 'the more overwhelming spirit in man.' Quoting St. Augustine that 'man is restless till he rests in God,' he said he 'did not have to be a Russian' to discover that he could not separate religion from daily life, could not 'dichotomize my work from my faith,' and that 'my Christianity and my humanity are one inseparable whole.' He confessed a 'restless past' in which God seemed 'apart and unreachable' and prayer unnecessary, and described his present practice of speaking with Jesus in his thoughts each morning, holding that 'it is not what I ask of Him that really matters; it is what He tells me I should do that truly matters,' for 'I am but a servant of God. Nothing more.' His one wish for 1991 was to become more open to God's word so that daily he might do only what God willed -- 'Thy will be done' in his life, family, career, the Rotary Club of Manila and his country.
